questions.question: What does Cantor's diagonal argument show about $\mathbb N$ and $[0,1]$?
options: The interval $[0,1]$ is finite
Every real number is a natural number
There is no bijection between $\mathbb N$ and $[0,1]$
There is a bijection between $\mathbb N$ and $[0,1]$

questions.question: In the diagonal argument, why is the newly constructed sequence not equal to the $i$th listed sequence?
options: It uses no digits at all
It has fewer digits than the listed sequence.
It is chosen to differ from that sequence in the $i$th digit
It is placed before the first sequence

questions.question: What is the conclusion if a supposed complete list of binary expansions misses the diagonal sequence?
options: Binary expansions cannot represent numbers
The natural numbers are finite
The diagonal sequence must equal every row
The supposed list was not complete

questions.question: Which set is identified as uncountable by Cantor's diagonal argument?
options: $\mathbb N$
Every finite set

questions.question: What does “flipping the diagonal entries” accomplish?
options: It turns a sequence into a finite set
It sorts the listed numbers into increasing order.
It builds an object disagreeing with each listed one somewhere.
It makes every row identical

questions.question: If the diagonal digits of a binary list begin $0,1,1,0$, what could the first four digits of the flipped diagonal sequence be?
A constructed sequence $s^*$ differs from $s_7$ in the seventh digit. Can $s^*=s_7$?
options: Yes, because all binary sequences are equal
No, because equal sequences cannot differ in any digit
Yes, because only the first digit matters
No, because $s_7$ is not a sequence

questions.question: What does the diagonal argument say about a claimed list $s_1,s_2,s_3,\ldots$ of all binary expansions in $[0,1]$?
options: Every entry after $s_1$ is unnecessary
The first entry must be repeated forever
A binary expansion can be constructed that is not on the list
The list must contain only finitely many sequences

questions.question: If $s^*$ differs from every row in a proposed enumeration of $[0,1]$, what property of the enumeration fails?
options: Surjectivity onto all represented numbers
The use of natural-number labels
Injectivity into the list positions
The fact that rows have digits

questions.question: Which conclusion follows from “there is no bijection between $\mathbb N$ and $[0,1]$”?
options: $[0,1]$ has exactly one element
$\mathbb N$ is uncountable
$[0,1]$ is uncountable
$[0,1]$ is empty

questions.question: Why is it not enough for the diagonal sequence to differ only from the first few rows?
options: A sequence is determined by finitely many digits
Rows after the first few are automatically empty
Only the first row matters in a countability proof
To refute a complete list, it must differ from every listed row

questions.question: What assumption is contradicted in the diagonal argument?
options: That natural numbers exist
That finite sets have finitely many elements.
That binary digits can be changed
That the interval can be listed by natural numbers.

questions.question: Why is the argument called “diagonal”?
options: It uses the $i$th digit of the $i$th listed sequence
It sorts numbers by their distance from the origin
It requires drawing a diagonal line in the real plane
It only applies to diagonal matrices

questions.question: Suppose $s^*$ is built so that its $k$th digit differs from the $k$th digit of $s_k$. What happens if someone claims $s^*=s_k$?
options: The claim is true if the first $k-1$ digits agree
The claim is impossible because the two sequences differ in digit $k$
The claim cannot be discussed for infinite sequences
The claim is true because $s_k$ appears in the list

questions.question: If every function $f:\mathbb N\to[0,1]$ misses at least one element, which statement follows?
options: Every such function is bijective
$\mathbb N$ and $[0,1]$ have the same cardinality
No such function is surjective
$[0,1]$ is countable

questions.question: A list has diagonal bits $d_1,d_2,d_3,\ldots$. If $s^*_i=1-d_i$ for binary digits, which row is definitely different from $s^*$ in the third digit?
options: The third row
No row can be identified
The first row only
The second row only

questions.question: What larger cardinality conclusion is supported by the diagonal argument?
options: No two infinite sets can be compared
The natural numbers have larger cardinality than the real numbers
The real numbers and natural numbers have the same cardinality
The real numbers have strictly larger cardinality than the natural numbers

questions.question: Why does the diagonal construction defeat a proposed bijection rather than merely finding a new notation for an old row?
options: It uses the same diagonal digits as the original list.
It is declared new without checking any row
It changes only the name of the first sequence
The constructed sequence differs from each row in a specific digit.

questions.question: A proposed enumeration of $[0,1]$ is used to build a diagonal sequence $s^*$. If $s^*$ corresponds to a point of $[0,1]$, what contradiction is obtained?
options: It should be listed, but differs from every listed entry.
The enumeration has too many natural-number indices.
The interval contains only rational numbers
The sequence has no binary digits

questions.question: Which proposed conclusion is directly ruled out by Cantor's diagonal argument?
options: A finite set can be listed
$[0,1]$ can be enumerated as $r_1,r_2,r_3,\ldots$
Two equal sequences agree in every digit
$\mathbb N$ can be enumerated as $1,2,3,\ldots$
